content: Dysuria refers to the experience of pain during urination. This pain can manifest as discomfort, a burning sensation, or outright pain when passing urine. Symptoms of Dysuria Pain associated with dysuria may be localized to the area where urine exits the body, such as the urethra. Alternatively, it may be felt deeper within the body, such as behind the pubic bone, in the bladder, or in the prostate. Dysuria is a relatively common condition. Individuals experiencing painful urination may also feel an increased urgency to urinate more frequently. Causes of Dysuria The most common causes of painful urination include: Infections or inflammation within the urinary tract. Urethritis in men, often caused by sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea or chlamydia. In women and girls, dysuria may result from: Atrophic vaginitis, which involves changes in vaginal tissue during menopause. Genital herpes infections. Irritation of vaginal tissue due to exposure to bubble baths, perfumes, or lotions. Vulvovaginitis, which includes yeast infections or other infections affecting the vulva and vagina. Other potential causes of dysuria include: Interstitial cystitis, a chronic bladder condition. Prostatitis, or infection of the prostate. Radiation cystitis, which involves damage to the bladder lining from pelvic radiation therapy. High-Risk Groups Individuals at higher risk for dysuria include: Those with multiple sexual partners. Those engaging in sexual activity with an infected partner. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact a healthcare provider if: There is discharge or drainage from the penis or vagina. You are pregnant and experiencing painful urination. Painful urination persists for more than one day. You notice blood in your urine. You develop a fever. Diagnosis A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination and ask detailed questions about your symptoms and medical history. These questions may include: When did the painful urination begin? Does the pain occur only during urination, or does it persist afterward? Do you experience back pain? Are there any other symptoms, such as fever, abnormal urine odor, or changes in urine volume or frequency? Have you noticed blood in your urine? Are there any rashes or itching in the genital area? Have you had a history of bladder or kidney infections? Have you recently changed your brand of soap, detergent, or fabric softener? Have you had sexual intercourse with someone who may have gonorrhea or chlamydia? Have you undergone surgery or radiation therapy involving the urinary or sexual organs? Diagnostic tests may include: Urinalysis to examine the urine for signs of infection or abnormalities. Urine culture to identify specific pathogens. If there is a history of bladder or kidney infections, a more detailed medical history, physical examination, and additional laboratory studies may be required. For women with vaginal discharge, a pelvic examination and analysis of vaginal fluids are necessary. Men with penile discharge may require a urethral swab for further evaluation. Treatment Options Treatment for dysuria depends on the underlying cause. For example, infections may require antibiotics, while other conditions may need specific interventions. Prognosis The outlook for dysuria depends on the underlying cause. Prompt diagnosis and treatment typically lead to resolution of symptoms. Possible Complications Complications of untreated dysuria may include: Cystitis (bladder infection). Pyelonephritis (kidney infection). Urinary tract infections (UTIs). Prevention To reduce the risk of dysuria caused by bacterial infections: Drink several glasses of water daily to flush bacteria from the bladder. Women should wipe from front to back after bowel movements to prevent bacterial spread. Women should urinate after sexual intercourse to reduce the risk of infection. To prevent dysuria caused by irritation: Women should keep the genital area clean and dry. Change tampons and sanitary napkins frequently. Avoid using irritating soaps, vaginal sprays, and douches. For female children: Limit bubble baths. Wash thoroughly but gently after playing in sand or water. Avoid prolonged play in wet swimsuits, as this can lead to irritation and redness of the vulva (vulvitis). To prevent dysuria caused by sexually transmitted infections: Avoid sexual activity or maintain a monogamous relationship with one uninfected partner. If you have multiple sexual partners or suspect your partner may be infected, use latex condoms during sexual activity.
